beats.beat: The company operates in two segments: creation of infrastructure and operating a ready mix concrete plant.

On the infrastructure side, the work spans railways — designing and constructing platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and laying railway tracks — bridges of several types, and bituminous and concrete roads.
The second business is a ready-mix concrete manufacturing facility at Kashimira in Thane district, Maharashtra, where the company has invested in machines and quality-control systems.

Revenue comes from winning tenders. The client floats a tender, holds a pre-bid meeting, bids are evaluated, and the work is awarded to the lowest quote after a Letter of Acceptance; the contractor then deposits a performance guarantee and takes site handover.

The client list is dominated by government and railway entities: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, MMRDA and the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, among private names.
Western Railway has been a client since 2006 and has been a major contributor to revenue; the company says its key customers accounted for 57% of total revenue in the year ended March 31, 2018.
Execution is concentrated in Mumbai and Maharashtra, with the company describing itself as a major player in Mumbai infrastructure through a healthy order book.

beats.beat: The restated numbers, converted from lakhs to crore, run from FY14 to FY18. Revenue fell from ₹86.61 crore in FY14 and ₹90.21 crore in FY15 to ₹60.53 crore in FY18.
The table below is the backbone of this section: revenue, profit before interest, depreciation and tax, net profit after adjustments, and borrowings for all five reported years.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — the closest line in the restated statement to EBITDA — moved from ₹9.46 crore in FY15 to a low of ₹6.76 crore in FY17, then recovered to ₹9.29 crore in FY18.
Net profit after adjustments was just ₹0.16 crore in FY17 and rose to ₹3.15 crore in FY18; earlier years were ₹0.33 crore, ₹0.78 crore and ₹0.96 crore.
The balance sheet is dominated by short-term borrowings of ₹35.37 crore in FY18, against long-term borrowings of ₹1.33 crore.
The company itself flags negative cash flow in recent financial years and slow recovery of trade receivables as a risk; the exact cash-flow figures are not in the extracted pages.

beats.beat: The promoter is Amit Bholanath Mishra, also the Managing Director; he holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of pre-issue share capital.
Three whole-time directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — hold 300 equity shares each; key management personnel Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the company.

The filing states none of the directors are on the RBI list of wilful defaulters and no criminal cases have been filed against directors; it also discloses pending litigation involving the company, promoter and directors.

Related-party transactions are disclosed: ₹68.4 lakh of loans taken from KMP or board members in FY18, ₹57.7 lakh of director remuneration, and ₹324.3 lakh of outstanding payables to related parties as of March 31, 2018.

Process flags: no independent agency appraised the proposed project, there is no monitoring agency for issue proceeds, equity shares were issued in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price, and two promoter companies — Al-Noor Chickens and A B Magma Automobiles — were struck off by the ROC in 2016 for non-operation.

beats.beat: The DRHP situates the company inside the infrastructure and construction sector — power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development.
It calls the market highly fragmented and working capital intensive, contributing roughly 8% to India's GDP at constant prices.

The growth story it cites includes Government flagship programmes such as 100 Smart Cities, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All, eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including construction, rising urbanisation, and India's projected need for ₹50 trillion in infrastructure investment by 2022.

It also points to a logistics sector expected to grow at 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020, and FDI of US$24.67 billion into construction development between April 2000 and December 2017.
The headwinds are in the company's own SWOT analysis: slow pace of government projects, working capital crunch affecting profitability, and changes in government policies.
Competition is described as present in both the organized and unorganized sectors, but the extracted pages do not name any competitor company.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-based construction company with two businesses: it executes civil infrastructure contracts — mainly railways, roads and bridges — and it runs a ready-mix concrete plant in Thane.
It is raising money through an SME-board IPO of 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; the issue price is not yet set, and the stated use of proceeds includes ₹11.30 crore for working capital.
The business is heavily concentrated: Indian Railways was its largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in FY18, and Western Railway alone accounts for 52% of the orders on hand.
Revenue has been falling — ₹90.21 crore in FY15 to ₹60.53 crore in FY18 — while net profit after adjustments swung from ₹0.16 crore in FY17 to ₹3.15 crore in FY18.

intro.purpose: Orient the reader in three moves: who this company is, what it is raising, and the two facts that should frame everything else — customer concentration and a declining revenue base that only recently turned profitable.

beats.beat: The issue is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, at an issue price to be determined.
The lead manager is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.
The stated object of the issue is to meet working capital requirements of ₹11.30 crore, with the balance for general corporate purposes at an amount not disclosed in the filing excerpts.

Two process cautions are disclosed: the company has not appointed any independent agency to appraise the project, and there is no monitoring agency for deployment of funds — the Audit Committee will monitor instead.
The extracted pages do not spell out whether the 44,28,000 shares are entirely a fresh issue or include an offer for sale; no selling shareholder is named in the digest.

offer.heading: The issue and what the money is for
offer.purpose: Lay out the concrete terms of the offer — size, bankers, objects — and flag what the DRHP does not disclose, including the fresh-issue vs offer-for-sale split.

beats.beat: One customer group drives the business. Indian Railways contributed 57% of FY18 revenue and Western Railway alone is 52% of the orders on hand; the filing itself says losing that customer would cause a significant dip in revenue.

Revenue has declined from ₹90.21 crore in FY15 to ₹60.53 crore in FY18, and the company warns it had negative cash flow in recent financial years; the profit recovery in FY18 sits on top of a shrinking top line.

The model depends on winning government tenders. Revenue depends on acceptance of bids, an unsuccessful bid season directly hurts results, and the order book is not a reliable promise of future revenue because contracts can be adjusted, cancelled or suspended.

The balance sheet is short-term funded. Short-term borrowings were ₹35.37 crore in FY18, and the company had ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured loans repayable on demand as of March 31, 2018 — a repayment demand could hit cash flow and profitability.

Process and disclosure gaps are themselves a risk: no independent appraisal or monitoring agency for the project, continued related-party transactions, equity issued in the past 12 months at a possibly lower price, and two promoter companies struck off by the ROC.

risks.heading: What could go wrong
risks.purpose: Five specific, non-boilerplate risks drawn from the filing: customer concentration, shrinking revenue and cash flow, tender dependence, short-term debt structure, and governance and process gaps.

beats.beat: The pricing-basis table in the DRHP carries earnings per share of ₹1.31 for FY16, ₹0.63 for FY17, and ₹12.59 basic / ₹3.82 diluted for FY18; net asset value per share is ₹4.14, ₹1.97 and ₹28.14 for those years.
The DRHP says the issue price will be justified in consultation with the lead manager against these accounting ratios; the face value is ₹10 per share and the issue price is [●] times face value.
